chapters.title: EP 1 - Strange grasshopper
chapters.content:
The little house butler in this house is strange.

He goes out every day—

but never brings back a single mouse.

Foolish.

Today, just like any other day, the little butler failed to catch any prey.
The big woman butler fed him.
The little butler sat on the wooden platform, set a small table in front of him, and did something called homework.

I was waiting.
Waiting for him to finish his homework and bring out something to eat—or maybe a fun toy.

I was sunbathing on the porch when something like a grasshopper hopped over the wall.
It bounced and fluttered—perfectly shaped for a toy.

As usual, I approached to play the game of catching grasshoppers.
But this one looked... strange.
Like a wooden stick.
Like a grasshopper missing something.
A thin blue-green body, eyes too big for its size, and sharp-looking front legs raised like a boxer's guard.

I crept closer to inspect it.

Then this insane grasshopper attacked first—
a quick jab, a sucker punch.

I dodged lightly, like a proper cat, and threw a jab of my own.
The punch landed, but for some reason my paw started stinging.

I threw a few more punches.
This thing didn't seem to feel anything.
It even came at me harder, which was almost laughable.

But it wasn't fun anymore, and my paw just kept stinging,
so I went back to my spot, lay down, and returned to sunbathing.

Then the little butler stood up.
He strode over, grabbed the blue grasshopper with his bare hand, threw it over the wall, and said to me,

"Hey, Catherine.
Are you even a cat?
Can't even live up to your size... sheesh."

And then he went back to his homework.

That evening, I asked Navi, the cat next door.
He told me it was a praying mantis.

"A grasshopper with a bad temper and no flavor at all," he said.

Today was a humiliating day for me, as a cat.

chapters.title: EP 2 - Rooster
chapters.content:
When I stayed at home,
the big woman butler fed me.

Most days,
I ate whatever the little butler ate—
rice and side dishes.

The best days were when mackerel appeared.
From early morning,
a heavenly smell rose from the grill.

I always worried
he might eat it all.

But if I waited long enough,
even the meat on the bones
was enough.

Sometimes,
he left me a few slices of sausage.

Humans understand loyalty.
Humans understand cats.

At dawn,
the rooster cried.

Loud.
As if he owned the place.

The big woman went into the coop
and came back with eggs.

On those days,
I got one.

The coop smelled terrible.
I didn't like going near it.

But sometimes,
when I failed to catch a mouse—
and felt hungry—
I went there anyway.

Today,
the rooster caught me.

He was bigger than me.
Stronger.

My paws did nothing.
His beak was faster.

Something kept hitting me.
My fur came loose.
My head rang.

This was not food.

This was a mistake.

I ran.

Then the little butler came.

He swung a stick.
The rooster ran.

Back into the coop.

The little butler said,
"We might have chicken soup tonight."

I think
I will eat well tonight.

It hurts.

But
it is a good day.

chapters.title: EP 3 - Snow
chapters.content:
I hate winter.

When the cold wind slips between my fur,
my body grows slow,
and I wander, searching only for warm places.

When I sneak into the butler's room,
he gets angry.

"Didn't I build you a house already?"

He kicks me out.

There's no choice.
I go back outside.

Today, snow is falling.

Cold things drift down from the sky, slowly,
land on my fur, melt away,
and leave me feeling as miserable
as if I've been caught in the rain.

Worse still, when I place a paw on the white ground,
there's a sharp sting—like an electric shock—
and before I know it, I leap into the air.

Right paw.
Left paw.
Front paws.
Back paws.

I try to touch the ground as little as possible.

The dog beside me runs around too,
his paws hurting from the cold.

I cry in front of the butler's room.

Then the big woman butler comes out.

"Honey! Let her sleep in the corner tonight!"

The young boy butler answers,

"I got it. Take care of her."

She lays down a warm cushion
and a small blanket in the corner of the room.

The big woman butler is strange.

She calls the young boy butler "Honey."

When he leaves in the morning,
carrying heavy bags to somewhere unknown,
his heartbeat feels slow.
He looks unhappy.

But when he comes back,
his heartbeat becomes fast.

And there's a faint scent in the air—
a smell that somehow makes everything better.

I asked Navi next door about it.

She said it's called a "married couple."

Humans, she said, live together
after a man and a woman who love each other get married.

We cats groom each other when we like one another.

But those butlers don't groom at all.

When the little man butler says,

"Let's steam some hobang,"

the woman butler runs to the kitchen
and comes back with bread still breathing steam.

There are several pieces.

But she picks up just one,
blows on it—hoo, hoo—
and puts it into his mouth.

As he eats and talks,
she laughs.

Outside, snow piles up quietly.

Inside, their conversation never ends.

Maybe because they don't groom each other,
people call the little butler
"Little Groom."

It's warm.

I'm sleepy.

I want to sleep here again tomorrow.

chapters.title: EP 4 - Balloon Cat
chapters.content:
Warm winds blow, but sometimes the day turns cold.

Today I went near the water again.

Flowers were blooming there.
Frogs were hopping around,
so I chased them and played.

On the way home, I stopped by Navi's house.
Something smelled like it was burning.
In Navi's backyard were white wooden boxes,
each about the size of a doghouse.

An adult human stood there,
wearing something like a mesh veil over their head,
opening the lids of the wooden boxes
while smoke drifted from a smoker.
They were checking the bees' wax.

The buzzing noise annoyed me,
and I was tired,
so I jumped up onto the wall to head home.

The moment I landed,
something stung me—
sharper than when the rooster pecked me last time.
I must have been stung by a bee.

Limping on my front paw,
I followed the wall
and jumped down into the flower bed behind my house.

Then—
"zzzzzz~~~~~"
I was stung again.

This time, on my nose.

Being stung twice in one day hurts too much.

The adult female butler saw me
and rubbed toothpaste on me.
She muttered something like
"bee venom neutralizer... acidic... alkaline..."

I hated the smell of the toothpaste.
Even mice would run away from it.

Hunting will be difficult for a while.

In the evening, the little butler came home.
After washing up and eating,
he looked at me and laughed.

"Balloon Cat!!! You can fly without wings!!!"

The female butler next to him laughed too.

That night, Navi's human came over and said,
"This is good when you catch a cold,"
and gave us a jar of honey.

Humans really live by eating the most unnecessary things.

chapters.title: EP 5 - Another life
chapters.content:
Part 1 : Thrown away

It was around evening.

The female butler brought me a bowl of water. A strange chemical smell rose from it. Without realizing it, by pure instinct, I struck her hand.

Startled, the female butler stepped back and clasped her right hand with her left. The little butler was watching.

He checked her hand and said, "Let's disinfect it and put medicine on," then led her into the room.

It was time for dinner. I waited, wondering why no food was coming.

Beside me, Nurungi spoke. "Looks like there won't be dinner tonight."

I thought I'd misheard. "What do you mean, no dinner?"

Nurungi replied, "You still don't get the situation? Remember last time, when the rooster lunged at the master and ended up on the dinner table that evening? This house chose its baby."

Again, I thought I'd misheard. "The rooster attacked. And the little butler went in quietly."

Nurungi snorted. "That's why it's scarier. This isn't something that ends with a beating, idiot."

A moment later, the little butler came out.

His breathing wasn't rough, but there was a quiet, heavy force around him. I couldn't run.

Unlike usual, he grabbed the back of my neck and walked toward the front gate.

"You are free. Get out of my territory," he said, shut the door, and went back inside.

From the house came the sounds of preparing dinner, and the smell of food spread through the air.

When I climbed over the wall, Nurungi's leash had been taken off. Just moments ago we were friends, but now he barked at me with hostility.

If I went near the house, he would bite me.

I wandered around the yard. Hungry, with nowhere to go, I went to Nabi.

Nabi looked at me and sneered. "What brings a homeless stray cat here now?"

I asked Nabi, "Weren't we friends~~?"

Nabi answered, "Friends? That was only when your little butler was around. You were thrown away because you're tasteless and useless."

I said, "Why am I useless? I catch a lot of mice."

Nabi snorted. "Your little butler doesn't need cats to catch mice anymore. They've developed some strange new chemical. Put it in the warehouse and all the mice die. You didn't even know that?"

I asked, "Then what am I?"

Nabi said, "You're just a cat. A useless, ill-mannered cat. If your little butler wanted to, he could bring home as many other cats as he liked. I don't want to talk to a stray anymore. Don't come here again."

With that, Nabi went back into his house.



Part 2 : Territory

After hearing what Nabi said,
I went to the grain warehouse.
I'm a cat,
that place is my territory.

But it felt different from the warehouse I had seen during the day.
There were no workers,
no lights.

Behind the warehouse,
between the wall and the storage building,
there was a narrow alley.
Back when I came here with my butler,
there had been grass,
places where I could hide prey.

I jumped over the wall
and landed in the warehouse yard.

Then I heard voices—
the voices of unfamiliar cats.

A white-furred cat approached me.
"Who are you?
Do you know what happens
when you enter someone else's territory?"

I said,
"This is my territory.
Why are you the intruders?
Get out. Now."

One of the white cat's companions tilted his head and stepped closer.
"Your territory?
Then shouldn't you have marked it?
That's the rule among cats, isn't it?"

I looked around
and sniffed the air.

There was no trace of my scent.
Only the smell of the cats standing in front of me.

For a moment, I was afraid.

I stepped back and said,
"My little butler said this place was mine."

The other cats sneered.
"That's the problem with house cats.
They trust their owners
and think that makes them strong."

They began circling me slowly.

Then, suddenly,
one of them lunged at me,
bit into my side,
and started clawing.

It hurt too much.
I was terrified.
Crying, I ran.

I had nowhere to go.

I headed for the pine grove in the neighborhood.
There was a large stone there.
I thought I could hide beneath it.

On the way, I passed in front of my former butler's house.
Nurungi growled at me.

In every alley I passed,
there were cats.
I was beaten,
chased,
and beaten again,
until I barely made it to the pine grove.

An old cat was already sitting on the stone
where I had planned to rest.

He looked at me and said,
"I heard there was a cat thrown out today.
So it was you."

"I wasn't thrown out," I said.

The old cat laughed.
"That's what everyone says at first.
This is my spot.
Find somewhere else."

He bared his yellowed fangs.

I slipped between the large stones
and sat down.

The bite burned.
The bruises throbbed.
My stomach ached with hunger.

I looked up at the sky.
The moonlight was bright.

The only thing that hadn't changed
was that moonlight.

I remembered a song
I used to hear at my old butler's house.

"Memory!
Not a sound from the pavement.
Has the moon lost a memory?
She is smiling alone."



Part 3 : Survival

It was spring, but the night had been bitterly cold.
Drenched in morning dew, my body temperature dropped,
and I barely had the strength to move.
Only when the sun climbed to the middle of the sky
did my mind finally clear enough to think.

More than anything, I was hungry.
I needed to catch even the smallest insects in the grass.
That was when the old cat I had seen the night before
motioned ahead and said, "Follow me."
I glanced around, cautious, and trailed after him.

We went past the grass to the rice paddies behind it.
Water flowed between the ridges.
The old cat stepped into the shallow water.

He leapt—
a frog startled and jumped.
He caught it and ate it.

I, too, kept hopping along the water's edge,
and whenever a frog appeared, I caught and ate it.

Then he waited quietly by the water.
When small fish passed beneath the surface,
he struck them and flung them up onto the ridge.
I waited as well, watching for fish to pass.
After several attempts, I finally caught one and ate it.

He warned me:
if I went too close to the village,
the stray cats would be waiting.
If I went too close to the mountains,
I would become food for terrifying owls or weasels.

I listened.
I survived like that for several days.
Then one day, it rained.
Trying to escape the rain, I went near people's houses in the village,
only to be beaten by other cats and humans and sent back.

The old cat slept in the rain.
He never got up again.
A few days later, people placed his cold body in a trash bin and carried it away.
The stone he had guarded became mine,
but on rainy days, it was unbearable.

From somewhere nearby came the smell of cooked rice.
When I followed it, there was an old woman.
Sheltering from the rain under the eaves,
I watched her cook.
After a while, she carried the meal inside her room.

Wanting to feel even a little warmth from the kitchen,
I slipped in quietly and crouched in front of the hearth.
I must have fallen asleep.

Suddenly, a flash and a sharp pain woke me.
The old woman was holding a fire poker, shouting,
"You thieving cat! Get out of here!"
I ran away.

Still, when night came,
I would return to that place, sleep there in secret, and leave before dawn.

One day, she caught me.
The old woman began striking me with a switch of twigs.
I cried out with everything I had.
Then the old man came out briefly and said,
"A life that enters to survive should not be treated that way."
He tossed me a lump of food.

Whenever it rained, I went back to that house.
The old man would push me under the wooden floor.
"At least here, you'll be able to avoid the rain."

When summer arrived,
food became plentiful—

butterflies, moths, crickets, frogs, even squirrels.
Perhaps my hunting skills had improved as well.
From time to time, I caught and ate minnows
and even loaches, and lived on that way.

chapters.title: EP 6 - Real Cat!
chapters.content:
All summer long, I ran, hunted, and climbed trees.

Some things I could eat.
Some things I could not.

Some places I could go.
Some places I had to avoid.

When other cats came too close
to where I hunted or slept,
I lost everything.

Even the old couple's house—
where I slipped in on rainy days—
was something I had to protect.

One day, I returned to the stream
where I had once followed the old cat.

The current was fast.
The water was deep.
I stood there for a long time,
then turned back.

On my way home,
I saw a group of stray cats gathered together.

Before, I would have run
or taken a long way around.

But that day,
my paws carried me toward them.

They noticed me.

They tensed.

I moved closer.

They weren't looking at me.

A praying mantis.

Whenever one of them stepped closer,
it struck—
sharp, fast.

They froze.

I stepped forward.

I remembered.

A hand.
A quick movement.

I feinted with my paw,
jumped onto its back,
and bit the back of its neck.

It struggled.

Its forelegs cut through the air.

But it wasn't enough.

I pinned it down.

"This thing has a bad temper," I said.
"And it doesn't taste good."

"If you want it, eat it.
I'm going back."

I turned.

Behind me—

"You are a real cat!!"

"She's a real cat..."

"So cool."

"Come play next time."

I stopped.

A warmth rose in my chest.

"Sure," I said.
"But I have to hunt."

"Next time."

I went back.

That night, I was alone again.

But the words stayed with me.

"REAL CAT."

I slept well.

chapters.title: EP 7 - Spring Rain
chapters.content:
Sometimes, I spent time with stray cats.

Sometimes we went down to the stream together,
catching frogs and fish.

As we crossed one another's territories,
we learned it was not an invasion—
just overlapping lives.

That year, after a brutal winter had passed,
one spring day,
we were hunting a snake together.

To us cats, a snake is no real match.

It strikes slowly, clumsily,
while we take turns—
darting in, landing a hit, and slipping away.

Our claws and teeth never sank in,
but the blows landed heavy.

There was a certain pleasure in it.

I wanted to play a little longer,
but the snake grew exhausted
and collapsed.

We grabbed it in our mouths
and went behind a lumber mill.

We shared the prey
and groomed one another.

That was when
we caught the scent of an unfamiliar cat.

One of us stepped forward.

The stranger was trembling.

"This is my territory.
My human told me so."

One of my friends replied,
"If this is your territory,
why isn't your scent here?"

The stranger couldn't answer.

My friends chased him away.

Ah—

I laughed.

"You guys! You should be kind!!!"

They answered,
"We avoided the vital spots and went easy!
You know that, don't you?!"

I said,
"We all know.
Me too. You too."

We nodded.

Later, I was resting on my rock—
my rock,
in my territory.

That same stranger approached.

I climbed onto the rock.

"Your human abandoned you, didn't they?!"

"They didn't abandon me...
they just let me out of the car."

"At first, everyone says that.

Go over there—
where the rocks are piled up."

He curled up
and fell asleep among the stones.

The next day, I went to see him.

He was soaked with morning dew,
curled tightly into himself.

I woke him.

I showed him how I hunt—
how to catch frogs and fish in the ditch,
how to catch squirrels in the trees.

Then one day,
after spending time with the others,
on my way back to my territory,

I ate from a bowl left outside.

When I returned to my rock,
my stomach twisted,
and my head spun.

I sat down.

Rain began to fall.

Cold drops soaked my fur,
soaked my body.

I should have taken shelter.

But I didn't.

I stayed.

I grew sleepy.

I fell asleep.

It was a dream—

warm.

Warm like the arms
of my former butler.
